You know, when I got sick in my early 20's I felt like I had a virus all the time and was fatigued. Since a viral source couldn't be identified, it got called "Chronic Fatigue Syndrome," and then I got to read article after article telling me that since current medical knowledge couldn't explain a cause that I wasn't really sick, and this was "all in my head".

So then, just before I reached 30, we discovered that food was the cause of the viral symptoms and the persistent fatigue (my immune system was being triggered by common things in the food I was eating, and that led to the viral symptoms and the lethargy). Specifically, cutting things like gluten out of my diet seemed to lessen the problems. However, nobody really understands why that works at the moment. So once again, I am being told that since the mechanism for gluten sensitivity isn't understood that this is "all in my head".

You know something, at this point I am just going to call BS on that. There are going to be some gastrointestinal and autoimmune problems that will be cured by cutting gluten out of the diet and some that are cured by cutting other triggers out of the diet. I think it is better that scientists and doctors try to understand the causes of various issues instead of explaining away their ignorance by pretending that patients are just "making it up" when they don't really understand what is going on. The real question isn't why 30% of the population is crazy for thinking that gluten is harming them, the real question is what is gluten doing to people that has led 30% of the population to believe that they are better off without it.

I think if anyone stops eating bread and croissants and spaghetti they will start to feel better than they did when they ate those things. That being said, what you're describing actually sounds like celiac to me, I assume you're 100% sure you don't have celiac disease (or some form of it). I'm absolutely not a medical professional or dietician, but fatigue and viral symptoms (stomach?) are symptoms of celiac disease. I work in the restaurant industry in a liberal state, there is a huge gluten-free trend right now occurring and I don't believe for a second that its absolutely necessary for all the people participating. What I do know is that I've run into one person in the bakery who said she had celiac disease and wouldn't even touch any of the gluten-free options because she knows even a few molecules will affect her. I'm not saying I don't think gluten intolerance is a thing, for the record.

Edit: omitted two "absolutely"s

It is definitely not celiac; for the first 20 years of my life I had no sensitivity to gluten at all and ate bread all the time with absolutely no perceivable ill effects. What I think is the cause is that I used Accutane in my late teens which has been linked to severe gastrointestinal problems. So now after experiencing exposure to such a toxic chemical I am sensitive to certain types of foods, and gluten appears to be one of the harshest culprits (and I am not alone, hence, the trend...even "normal" people don't want to eat something that has been linked to harsher symptoms for people with gastrointestinal issues).

Since so many doctors were calling me crazy for having chronic fatigure, I actually went and got a degree in biochemisty to help treat myself. From what I have read on celiac disease, the current line of thinking is that the issue is caused by a "leaky gut". What they think happens is that gluten either passes through or more likely can bind to the damaged small intestine which then recruits the immune system to come in and remove it (this very same "sticky" property is exactly why it is used in bread). So the theory is that gluten insensitivity is first caused by some sort of damage to the small intestines, then certain molecules such as gluten recruit the immune system when ingested which produces the viral symptoms and fatigue (it becomes a "chronic" problem if you don't watch your diet and continue to eat bread every day).

Now, the question everyone wants to know is, does the gluten itself cause the membrane damage? That I do not know. At least in the case of celiac disease it is usually genetic or in my case I was exposed to a hazardous chemical that likely created the damaged small intestine. Then eating gluten merely triggers the immune system causing the disease symptoms (gluten in these situations wouldn't cause the problem, but would draw out the symptoms). I have no reason to believe at this point that people with healthy small intestines that do not show any ill effects from eating gluten are in danger. Having said that, I know that I don't know if it is dangerous or not, so I can see why people are being cautious. Especially when we have authorities calling sick people "crazy" every time they don't understand why they are sick.
